draft.title: Proof by contrapositive
card: A statement of the form "if P then Q" has a contrapositive: "if not Q then not P". Swap the two parts, then negate both.
A statement and its contrapositive are logically equivalent. Both are true or both are false. So proving the contrapositive proves the original.
Use this method when not Q gives you something easier to work with than P does. It is often so when Q is a negative claim such as "n is not even" or "n is odd".

Example: prove that if n² is even, then n is even. The contrapositive is: if n is not even, then n² is not even. Let n = 2k + 1. Then n² = 4k² + 4k + 1 = 2(2k² + 2k) + 1, which is odd. So the contrapositive is true, and so is the original.
draft.remember: To prove if P then Q, prove if not Q then not P. The two are equivalent.

a.q: What is the contrapositive of "if x is a multiple of 6, then x is even"?
opts: If x is not even, then x is not a multiple of 6
If x is even, then x is a multiple of 6
If x is not a multiple of 6, then x is not even
If x is not a multiple of 6, then x is even
a.why: Swap the two parts and negate both: not even comes first, and not a multiple of 6 follows. The option that only swaps the parts is the converse, which is a different statement and need not be true.
a.clue: Swap the parts, then negate both.

b.q: To prove "if n² is odd, then n is odd" by contrapositive, which statement should be proved?
opts: If n is even, then n² is even
If n is odd, then n² is odd
If n² is even, then n is even
If n² is odd, then n is even
b.why: P is "n² is odd" and Q is "n is odd". The contrapositive is "if not Q then not P": if n is even, then n² is even. The option "if n² is even, then n is even" is the converse of the negated parts in the wrong order, so it does not prove the original.
b.clue: Not odd means even. Put not Q first.

a.best: If x is not even, then x is not a multiple of 6

b.best: If n is even, then n² is even

problems.detail: The card says to use contrapositive when Q is a negative claim, giving 'n is odd' as an example of a negative claim. Calling 'odd' a negative claim is confusing. The worked example also does not fit the advice: there Q is 'n is even', which is not negative, and the real reason the method helps is that P ('n² is even') is hard to use directly.

Why (b) calls 'if n² is even, then n is even' 'the converse of the negated parts in the wrong order'. That is muddled. This statement is the inverse (if not P then not Q), and the why should name it as such.
